title: Approval record — the signed consent object (D44, C-5)
description: Outline from goal-file-schema-reconciliation-2026-08-15.md §11 (§18 item 1), extended at v7 for B2's standing modes and X-trust-06 (issue 64); not this document's tested surface — §14.2 review and the fixture set land with the family, not this pass. The signed object is the JCS bytes of this record with `signature` removed (C-5, replacing E1 §5.1's hash-concatenation formula, whose optional briefing member was an encoding-ambiguity hazard). DC-2 applies in full to `per-change` records: per-target validity, device nonce, monotonic-counter single use, persisted rejects. Standing records drop only the per-change nonce (L5, B2; an active enrolment carries its own device nonce, R3) and keep the rest of DC-2: per-target validity (`host`), single use as a per-grant high-water mark (`application_seq`), and persisted rejects, which win over any grant. Grok's `H(projected_augments)` extension is dropped — with the device-side projector there is no shipped projection to bind (map §9 preamble). OPERATOR RULINGS built in (each recorded in AGENTS.md, Android item 5). 2026-11-19, issue 64 choosers: "3. Include all classes", "1. Reusable grant (Recommended)", "1. Owner-enrolled trusted signers (Recommended)", "1. Bind both fields (Recommended)" (X-trust-06 adopted). 2026-11-20, PR 75 review: R1 "1. Carve-out (Recommended)", R2 "1. One class per grant (Recommended)", R3 "1. Device nonce (Recommended)", R4 "1. Apply-without-yes modes (Recommended)", R5 "1. Role in goal file now (Recommended)", R6 "1. Ordinary only (Recommended)"; R7 "1. Add to carve-out (Recommended)" (`policy-tree` joins the R1 carve-out), R8 "1. Separate PR after 75 (Recommended)" (the issue 55 goal-file pattern fixes are a separate PR after PR 75, in the same v7 window with no extra bump), R9 "1. Accept, disclose (Recommended)", R10 "1. Bind to enrollment (Recommended)"; each is quoted where it bites, in `signer`, `nonce`, `class`, `developer_mode`, `not_after` and the goal file's `advisor_key_map`. 2026-11-26, issue #76 enforcement rulings: Item 6 Option B (identical redelivery at stored active generation receives zero-write delivery ack under authenticated equality and liveness checks), Item 15 (refuse downward or equal `version_bump` `new <= old` for both `standing-application` and `per-change` owner records), Item 17 (no hard maximum horizon cap on `not_after`; strict calendar parsing and clock-rollback fail-closed). LEAD PROPOSALS, not operator rulings (each is open to the operator, and each is labelled "(lead proposal)" where it is stated): terminal revocation per grant_id and what follows from it (honoured at any generation, wins equivocation, tombstones never deleted); most-restrictive-wins and its tie and edge rules; the hold-window timing rules and persist-at-intake; an owner's per-change accept staying available against a covering standing-refusal; the Ed25519 verification profile; approval records' downgrade floor; the reading of "trust root" for the R1 carve-out (R7 settled `policy-tree`). OPERATOR RULING R9, 2026-11-20, PR 75 review, "1. Accept, disclose (Recommended)": a standing grant knowingly delegates root-equivalent authority to its covered signers, because a covered change may add or alter a service or interlock that runs as root. Revocation or expiry stops only later applications and a pending hold; it never undoes code or state an earlier application already installed. Because that authority is root-equivalent, a covered signer can also, through the code it installs, alter the trust root, the replay store, the validator and the clock, so the R1 carve-out and revocation bind the approval path and not such code: a grant should be given only to a signer the owner would trust with root. Scope is host, class, signers and expiry; there is no per-domain scope (lead proposal), so a grant covers every domain its class reaches. ENFORCEMENT-TIME RULES stated in the field descriptions are implemented by the pure-stdlib reference enforcement engine in `bin/approval_enforce.py` and verified by `tests/approval/` (tracking list: https://github.com/frdminc/tendcf/issues/76); a static fixture cannot express replay, generation, revocation, precedence or crash-order behaviour, which depend on device state; the static constraints that can be written as schema are, and each has a negative fixture.

schema_version.description: Family version, shared with goal-file and goal-diff (§11). 7 adds `record_kind`, the two standing kinds, and `signer`/`sig_alg` on every record (X-trust-06): the B2 nonce-less shape and X-trust-06 share one bump, because both change what a v6 validator would accept and C-policy-01 wants one number per acceptance set; the role on the goal file's trust entries (R5) rides the same bump. The grouping was decided at the schema design review (PR 62 review Q4, "1. Decide at design review" handed the decision to that review). 8 (issues #99 + #94): the approval-record shape is unchanged; the family moves with `goal-file.schema.json` (launchd `domain`, exact launchd unit-writer labels, and launchd `tendcf-install`). 9 (issue #103): the approval-record shape is unchanged; the family moves with `goal-file.schema.json` (launchd 3-value `domain` enum: `system` | `user-gui` | `user-background`). Approval records have floor = ceiling (lead proposal): a v9 validator refuses an approval record below 9, however many older goal-file versions the compiler still reads; there is no older acceptance path for a consent record.

record_kind.description: Which consent object this is. `per-change`: the v6 record (one yes or no about one change, device nonce, `approval_seq`), plus `signer`/`sig_alg`. `standing-enrollment`: the owner's signed enrolment, update or revocation of one standing grant (B2), the reusable grant. `standing-application`: a covered signer's claim that one change is covered by a live grant; it carries no device nonce and no verdict, and is replay-checked against per-device state instead (ruling 2026-11-19, reusable grant with persistent per-device replay state).

host.description: The target key this record is valid for — DC-2's per-target validity. Every kind names exactly one host; a grant is never fleet-wide.

signer.description: X-trust-06 (adopted, operator ruling 2026-11-19, "1. Bind both fields (Recommended)"): the typed identifier of the key that produced `signature`, inside the signed bytes. The validator verifies with exactly this key and refuses the record unless, at verification time, the key is an entry of the right `role` in the device's trust root (the `device-trust` `advisor-key` entries of the currently applied (baseline) goal file, never the proposed one, which could otherwise add the key that approves it; operator ruling R5, 2026-11-20, PR 75 review, "1. Role in goal file now (Recommended)"): an `owner` key for `per-change` and `standing-enrollment`; for `standing-application`, a key named in `covered_signers` of the live generation of the grant, which outside developer mode must also be a `covered-signer` entry. In developer mode only, a covered signer may be a key the trust root does not hold: the owner's enrolment is then the source of trust for that key, for this host and this grant only, and the trust ends for later applications with revocation, expiry or a later generation that omits the key (R9: it does not undo what an earlier application installed). Outside developer mode naming a key never creates trust. An `owner` key never signs a `standing-application`, and a `covered-signer` key never signs a `per-change` or `standing-enrollment` record. The device's own `host` key is never a `signer` (enforcement-time rule, and a schema_lint cross-check on the examples): the software the gate constrains holds that key.

sig_alg.description: X-trust-06: the signature algorithm, inside the signed bytes. It MUST equal the algorithm the validator actually verified with and agree with the `signer` prefix (the typed key prefix is the only algorithm record the trust root holds; when a second algorithm is added, `sig_alg` and the prefix must name the same one); a mismatch is refused, never retried under another algorithm. Naming an algorithm never enables it: the enum is the approved set, and widening it is a schema_version bump. Ed25519 verification profile (lead proposal): RFC 8032 pure Ed25519, canonical encodings only (`S` below the group order, canonical public key and `R`), so the Python validator and the Kotlin agent accept the same signatures.

baseline_sha256.description: H(old canonical goal file). `per-change`: absent ONLY at first adoption, where there is no prior approved baseline to name — a named §14.2 review target (TC-11/TC-20 territory), not a property this outline claims to have fully worked out. `standing-application`: REQUIRED. The validator refuses an application whose baseline_sha256 is not the baseline currently applied on this host: an application carries no device nonce, so binding the baseline is its only freshness against state (a held-back application released after the owner accepted a later change is refused, never applied over it). First adoption is never by standing application (§9.4: first adoption is a baseline ceremony at first run). Not on `standing-enrollment`.

proposed_sha256.description: H(new canonical goal file) — what the record is about. `per-change` and `standing-application` only. A persisted reject (DC-2) of this hash wins over any standing grant: a change the owner refused stays refused until a later per-change accept.

nonce.description: Device-issued, single-use (DC-2). Present on `per-change` records and on `standing-enrollment` with `grant_state: active`; forbidden on a revocation and on a `standing-application`. Operator ruling R3, 2026-11-20, PR 75 review, "1. Device nonce (Recommended)": active enrolments carry a device-issued nonce, revocation is nonce-less. The device issues an enrolment's nonce only inside the on-device owner ceremony of the class that enrolment needs (see `class`, `developer_mode`). Installing an active enrollment requires a generation above the stored one and consumes its ceremony nonce exactly once. Identical redelivery at the stored active generation may receive a zero-write delivery acknowledgment only under the authenticated equality and liveness checks in `generation` (operator ruling 2026-11-26, issue #76 item 6 Option B). A signed enrolment that was never delivered, or one captured and replayed later after store loss or revocation, carries a nonce the device no longer holds and is refused: that is B1's "fresh" for an enrolment, and the evidence that the ceremony took place. A revocation carries none, because it must work while the owner is away from the device. An application carries none (L5, B2: the one check a standing mode drops). For an enrolment, the device binds each nonce it issues to the full scope the ceremony showed (`record_kind`, `host`, `grant_id`, `mode`, `covered_signers`, `class`, `developer_mode`, `hold_seconds`, `not_after`, and the ceremony level; PR 75 R4 #3) and refuses any other use, so a nonce from an `ordinary` ceremony never satisfies a `baseline` enrolment or a developer-mode one (R6). For a `per-change` record, the nonce binds to (`host`, `proposed_sha256`, `ceremony_class`, DC-2; PR 75 R4 #5). The set of outstanding nonces is part of the rollback-protected store (see `grant_id`). Each device nonce comes from a cryptographic random source with at least 128 bits of entropy, is never a counter and is never derived from replay-store state, so it is unique for the life of the host key across store loss, reflash and reinstall; R3 (freshness) and R10 (binding) rest on that. Exact byte encoding is residue, not decided here: the schema bounds the value at 22 to 128 printable ASCII characters (22 is the length of 128 bits in the narrowest common encoding, unpadded base64url) with no newline. That is a floor and an alphabet, not an encoding.

enrollment_nonce.description: `standing-application` only, and required. Operator ruling R10, 2026-11-20, PR 75 review, "1. Bind to enrollment (Recommended)": each application names the enrolment instance it relies on, here the `nonce` of the active enrolment, and the validator refuses an application whose `enrollment_nonce` is not the nonce stored with the grant at the stored generation. A re-enrolment of the same `grant_id` (after the store loss R3 provides for, or at generation 1 again) carries a fresh device nonce, so an application signed under an earlier enrolment names a nonce the device no longer holds and is refused, whatever its `generation` and `application_seq`; without this member the pair (`grant_id`, `generation`) is the only binding and an old application replays. It sits inside the signed bytes, so it cannot be swapped. It is not a secret: the covered signer is shown the enrolment it relies on. Forbidden on every other record kind. Same shape and the same entropy rule as `nonce`. A mismatch is refused before `application_seq` is persisted, so a wrong-nonce application can neither burn nor raise the mark.

approval_seq.description: Monotonic counter, DC-2 single-use: the validator rejects any `per-change` record whose approval_seq does not exceed the last persisted one for this host. `per-change` only; standing applications use `application_seq`, a separate counter per grant, so that an owner's yes and a covered signer's application never race for one number. At most 2^53-1: JCS numbers are IEEE doubles (RFC 8785), so a larger integer has no exact signed spelling.

briefing_sha256.description: Optional, `per-change` only: binds the record to the briefing bytes the person actually saw, when one was shown.

verdict.description: `per-change` only: what the approver decided about proposed_sha256. A reject is persisted (DC-2) and outlives any standing grant; refusing a change shown during a hold window is a `per-change` reject, and during a hold window such a reject signed by an owner key that names this host and this `proposed_sha256` stops the apply whatever its ceremony class, nonce or `approval_seq` (a hold window defaults to apply, so the owner's no must not be discardable on a technicality; any doubt during a hold window means the change does not apply — lead proposal, after the Fable review of PR 75). Such a reject is a `per-change` reject like any other: persisted (DC-2) and keyed on the exact `proposed_sha256`, so it also outlives the window; an old owner reject of the same hash replayed by a relay can only stop a later window, which only tightens.

refused.description: Hunk key-paths the refusal is annotated with. Present iff verdict is reject; annotation only — it does not change what was refused (all of it, §9.3's all-or-nothing rule), only explains why, so the proposer knows what to re-render.

ceremony_class.description: `per-change` and `standing-application`: asserted by the signer, checked against the validator's own DERIVED requirement (map §9.8) — a mismatch is refused, never silently upgraded or downgraded. For an application it must also equal the grant's `class` (no class implies another), and every hunk and every coverage change of the change must itself derive that class (a `version_bump` diff has neither, so a `baseline` grant covers the bump itself): a mixed-class application is refused, so a `privileged` grant never carries ordinary service or interlock hunks along with one privileged hunk (lead call, round 2 adversary finding 2).

grant_id.description: `standing-enrollment` and `standing-application`: names one grant on this host. The device keeps, per (host, grant_id), the highest enrolment generation it has accepted, that generation's state and scope, and the application high-water mark, together with the active enrolment's nonce, the set of outstanding device nonces, DC-2's `approval_seq` and the persisted rejects: the persistent per-device replay state. Operator ruling R3, 2026-11-20, PR 75 review, "1. Device nonce (Recommended)": that store must be rollback-protected (a restore from backup, a reflash, or a reinstall that keeps the host key must not be able to bring back an older copy), and loss of it, or any sign it was rolled back, voids every standing grant on the host (fail closed; re-enrolment by ceremony). Tombstones of revoked grant_ids are never deleted, since deleting one lets the old active enrolment back in (lead proposal).

generation.description: `standing-enrollment`: the grant's version. Installing an active enrollment requires a generation above the stored one and consumes its ceremony nonce exactly once. Identical redelivery at the stored active generation may receive a delivery acknowledgment only under the authenticated equality and liveness checks (operator ruling 2026-11-26, issue #76 item 6 Option B): strict duplicate-key-free JSON parse, valid canonical pure RFC 8032 Ed25519 signature, baseline `owner` role, matching `host`, live active grant (not tombstoned/revoked), not expired (`not_after`), stored canonical JCS-minus-signature bytes present (missing fails closed), and exact byte-for-byte equality with those stored JCS-minus-signature bytes; a verified identical redelivery performs zero writes, zero nonce/counter mutation, zero prompts, zero actuation, and zero changes to pending holds or `application_seq`, and returns the same success shape as initial acceptance. A second active enrolment at the stored generation with other signed bytes (the JCS bytes without `signature`, so whitespace/member-order differences or a re-encoded signature do not cause false equivocation) is refused (equivocation), so an old enrolment can never be replayed over a newer one. A revocation is honoured at ANY generation, wins any equivocation, and is accepted even for a grant_id the device has never seen (it stores the tombstone): `revoked` is terminal for the `grant_id`, so an active enrollment at any later generation for a tombstoned `grant_id` is refused (PR 75 R4 #1), and honouring revocation is replay-safe (lead proposal). `standing-application`: the generation it relies on, which must equal the stored, active generation — any re-enrolment or revocation strands every application made under an earlier one. At most 2^53-1 (RFC 8785 numbers are IEEE doubles); a grant at the top of the range can only be retired by revocation and replaced by a new grant_id.

grant_state.description: `standing-enrollment` only. `active` is a grant: it carries a device nonce and the full scope (`mode`, `covered_signers`, `class`, `developer_mode`, plus `hold_seconds` and `not_after` where required). `revoked` has its own minimal shape: only the common members, `grant_id`, `generation` and `grant_state` — the scope members and `nonce` are forbidden, so there is one spelling of a revocation and nothing on it to disagree with the stored grant. `revoked` is terminal for the grant_id: no later generation can reactivate it, and a new grant needs a new grant_id (lead proposal). In the public build a revocation is honoured as a record (Smaller 1; the separate developer build keeps its ignore-revoke override, AGENTS.md Android item 2), but what it stops is the future: OPERATOR RULING R9, 2026-11-20, PR 75 review, "1. Accept, disclose (Recommended)": a standing grant knowingly delegates root-equivalent authority to its covered signers, because a covered change may add or alter a service or interlock that runs as root. Revocation or expiry stops only later applications and a pending hold; it never undoes code or state an earlier application already installed. Because that authority is root-equivalent, a covered signer can also, through the code it installs, alter the trust root, the replay store, the validator and the clock, so the R1 carve-out and revocation bind the approval path and not such code: a grant should be given only to a signer the owner would trust with root. It needs only an owner-role signature — not the ceremony of the grant's class, and no device nonce, so it works while the owner is away from the device — and takes effect when it is persisted, before any further application is judged; a hold window pending for that grant ends without applying.

mode.description: `standing-enrollment` (active) only: the standing mode enrolled (B2). `standing-approval` applies a covered change without a per-change yes; `hold-window` shows it and applies it after `hold_seconds` unless the owner refuses first; `wait-for-user` holds a covered change until the owner answers per change; `standing-refusal` refuses covered changes. Every mode is owner-enrolled and refusable, and none is a default. Precedence (lead proposal): "covers" is evaluated over every active, unexpired grant on the host, not only the one an application names; when several cover one change the most restrictive wins (refusal, then wait-for-user, then hold-window, then standing-approval), and among hold-window grants the longest `hold_seconds` wins. An application naming a wait-for-user grant is parked for the owner's per-change answer, and one naming a standing-refusal grant is refused; neither is applied. An owner's own `per-change` accept of the exact `proposed_sha256` is a different object and stays available against a covering standing-refusal or wait-for-user grant: standing modes govern applications, and a persisted reject of that hash still wins over every grant. A persisted reject is keyed on the exact `proposed_sha256`, so a re-rendered file is a new proposal with a new hold window; the owner's remedy is revocation, which the hold-window screen should offer beside refuse.

hold_seconds.description: `standing-enrollment` with `mode: hold-window` only, and required there: how long a covered change is shown and refusable before it applies. Timing (lead proposal): the window runs from when the device first shows the change, on a monotonic clock that does not advance while the device is off or asleep; and at the moment of apply the device re-evaluates every check (grant still active, generation still equal, the `enrollment_nonce` still the grant's, `not_after`, persisted rejects, the covering set, the baseline still the applied one), not only at receipt. At most 2^53-1.

covered_signers.description: `standing-enrollment` (active) only: the keys whose applications this grant covers. Outside developer mode each must be a `covered-signer` entry in the trust root (ruling 2026-11-19, "1. Owner-enrolled trusted signers (Recommended)": any explicitly trusted enrolled signer, automation and organisational signers included); the grant scopes that trust, it never creates it. In developer mode (R6) a key may be one the trust root does not hold, and the owner's enrolment is then the source of trust for it, for this host and this grant only. An `owner` key is never listed, and the device's own `host` key is never listed (enforcement-time rule, and a schema_lint cross-check on the examples). Listed in ascending byte order of the string, so one grant has one spelling (a schema_lint check on the examples; a JSON Schema cannot compare members). The grantor is `signer`, an `owner` key.

class.description: `standing-enrollment` (active) only: the ceremony class this grant covers, exactly one. Operator ruling R2, 2026-11-20, PR 75 review, "1. One class per grant (Recommended)", with the 2026-11-19 ruling "3. Include all classes": every class may be covered, and each class is its own grant, enrolled separately and explicitly; nothing is implied by a higher class, and revocation is per class because it is per grant. A scalar, not an array, so there is no ordering of classes to rule on. The enrolment is accepted only through the owner ceremony of this class (at least the privileged ceremony when `developer_mode` is true, R6), so a grant can never cover more than its enrolment ceremony did. A standing application covers a change only if every hunk and every coverage change of it derives this class on its own, never the maximum over them (lead call, round 2 adversary finding 2; a `version_bump` diff has neither, so a `baseline` grant covers the bump itself). Entry-removal hunks in a domain whose coverage changes in the same diff are `ordinary` hunks, so retreating a populated domain is a mixed-class application and is never grantable by a standing application. OPERATOR RULING R9, 2026-11-20, PR 75 review, "1. Accept, disclose (Recommended)": a standing grant knowingly delegates root-equivalent authority to its covered signers, because a covered change may add or alter a service or interlock that runs as root. Revocation or expiry stops only later applications and a pending hold; it never undoes code or state an earlier application already installed. Because that authority is root-equivalent, a covered signer can also, through the code it installs, alter the trust root, the replay store, the validator and the clock, so the R1 carve-out and revocation bind the approval path and not such code: a grant should be given only to a signer the owner would trust with root. OPERATOR RULING R1, 2026-11-20, PR 75 review, "1. Carve-out (Recommended)": standing grants never cover changes to the trust root, owner/advisor keys, covered-signer trust, the validator binary/version or the grant replay state; those always need a per-change owner record. Other privileged and baseline changes stay grantable. Enforcement-time rule for the enforcement PR (and its negative list): a `standing-application` whose change touches any of those is refused, whatever the grant, and the change needs a `per-change` record from an `owner` key. Reading of the list (lead reading, not part of the ruling): the trust root and the owner/advisor and covered-signer key set are the `device-trust` `advisor-key` entries and their roles; the trust root also includes the `trust-policy` entry, which decides whether a local yes is required; the validator binary/version is the `agent` entry; the grant replay state is not expressible in a goal file and is on the carve-out too: no standing grant ever covers a change that would reach or reset it, and it needs a per-change owner record. OPERATOR RULING R7, 2026-11-20, PR 75 review, "1. Add to carve-out (Recommended)": `policy-tree` (the generic bundle's digest, the enforcer's own policy bytes) joins the carve-out: a standing application never covers a change to a `policy-tree` entry, and that change needs a per-change owner record, like the rest of the list. With R7 the list is: the `advisor-key`, `trust-policy`, `agent` and `policy-tree` entries of `device-trust`, and the grant replay state. Default-deny over `device-trust` (lead call, round 2 adversary finding 3, a tightening): every `device-trust` entry kind except `supervisor` is on the carve-out unless an operator ruling says otherwise, so a trust kind added later is carved out by default, and its version bump states its membership; the peer allowlist and the device resource policy (map §9.8) are trust root once they exist. Coverage transitions of an empty domain are grantable under a grant of the class they derive (PR 75 R4 #4, issue #76 item 14). Migrations and re-adoption (lead call, adversary finding 4, a tightening): a standing application of class `baseline` is refused unless the device can compute the `device-trust` content of the applied baseline and of the proposal under one schema and every carved-out entry is equal; a `version_bump` with `new` not above `old` is refused (operator ruling 2026-11-26, issue #76 item 15: downward or equal `version_bump` with `new <= old` is refused for both standing applications and `per-change` owner records); a migration that changes any `device-trust` entry, a role default included, and any re-adoption are never by standing application. Static expressibility: the change a record covers is a goal-diff hunk, not a member of the approval record, so no approval-record schema rule or fixture can express the carve-out (R1 and R7 alike); it stays an enforcement-PR negative-list item (https://github.com/frdminc/tendcf/issues/76).

developer_mode.description: `standing-enrollment` (active) only. `true` is Smaller 1's developer mode, ruled in the form of R6 (operator, 2026-11-20, PR 75 review, "1. Ordinary only (Recommended)"): developer_mode is true only on a grant whose `class` is `ordinary`, its enrolment needs at least the privileged owner ceremony, and `not_after` is required. A covered signer may then be one of the owner's choosing that the trust root does not hold, enrolled by this grant for this host only: the grant is the source of that trust, which ends for later applications with revocation, expiry or a later generation without it (not for what an earlier application installed; OPERATOR RULING R9, 2026-11-20, PR 75 review, "1. Accept, disclose (Recommended)": a standing grant knowingly delegates root-equivalent authority to its covered signers, because a covered change may add or alter a service or interlock that runs as root. Revocation or expiry stops only later applications and a pending hold; it never undoes code or state an earlier application already installed. Because that authority is root-equivalent, a covered signer can also, through the code it installs, alter the trust root, the replay store, the validator and the clock, so the R1 carve-out and revocation bind the approval path and not such code: a grant should be given only to a signer the owner would trust with root.), and the device shows a persistent indicator while any such grant is active. `false`: every covered signer must already be a `covered-signer` entry in the trust root (see `covered_signers`).

not_after.description: `standing-enrollment` (active) only: UTC instant after which the grant covers nothing. REQUIRED when `mode` is `standing-approval` or `hold-window` (operator ruling R4, 2026-11-20, PR 75 review, "1. Apply-without-yes modes (Recommended)": the modes that apply a change without a per-change yes), and when `developer_mode` is true (R6); optional for `wait-for-user` and `standing-refusal`, where expiry only returns the device to asking. Absent means until revoked. Expiry is the only bound on a withheld revocation or a stale, undelivered record; it rests on the device clock, so it is a bound, not a guarantee (clock rollback is an enforcement-time concern), and no stronger than the date the owner chose: a far-future date satisfies the requirement and bounds nothing (no maximum horizon is ruled). One spelling: `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ`, no fraction, no offset, ranges checked by the pattern and calendar validity by `format: date-time`; a validator that does not check formats must parse the value, and an unparseable or impossible value REFUSES the record, it is never read as absent.

application_seq.description: `standing-application` only: the per-grant replay counter. The initial stored mark is 0, so the first application is 1. The validator accepts an application only if application_seq exceeds the high-water mark stored for (host, grant_id), and it durably persists the new mark BEFORE it applies the change — for a hold-window grant, when it accepts the application and starts the hold, before the change is shown (lead proposal): a crash after the write and before the apply loses that application (fail closed; the signer re-issues with a higher number), and no crash can make one application apply twice. The mark never decreases, across generations included. Every check MUST pass before the mark is written (non-exhaustive list, PR 75 R4 #2 / issue #76 item 26: strict parse and schema, per-target `host`, `sig_alg` and canonical Ed25519 signature, baseline trust-root role, `covered_signers` membership, grant active and not tombstoned, `generation`, `enrollment_nonce`, `not_after` and clock rollback, persisted DC-2 rejects, `baseline_sha256` and `proposed_sha256` hash binding, R1/R7 carve-out, per-hunk derived class and `ceremony_class`, migration invariants, and covering-grant precedence such as `standing-refusal`), so a refused application can neither burn nor raise the mark. This keeps DC-2's single use while the grant itself is reused (reusable, not replayable). At most 2^53-1 (RFC 8785 numbers are IEEE doubles); a grant whose mark reaches the top can accept no more applications, and its recovery is a new grant_id.

signature.description: Detached signature by `signer` under `sig_alg` over the JCS bytes of this record with this member removed (C-5), so `signer` and `sig_alg` are signed. Exact encoding is residue, not decided here.

allOf.$comment: R4: the modes that apply a change without a per-change yes need an expiry.
R6: developer mode only on an ordinary grant, and only with an expiry.

key_id.description: A typed key identifier, the same form as `host`. No trailing newline: Python's `$` matches before one, and two spellings of one key are two answers in two validators (issue 55).

sig_alg.description: The approved signature algorithms. One today, matching the only key type `key_id` admits.

grant_id.description: Opaque grant name, unique per host; a restricted alphabet so it is one spelling on every surface (no trailing newline, as in `key_id`).
